title: AWS Cloud Foundations
description: Learn the core services of Amazon Web Services. Understand how to deploy scalable infrastructure without buying physical hardware.

lessons.title: What is Cloud Computing?
lessons.explanationHtml:
Cloud computing is simply renting someone else's computer. Instead of buying physical servers that sit idle 90% of the time, you pay Amazon, Microsoft, or Google for the exact CPU cycles and storage you use, billed by the second.

This allows startups to instantly scale to handle millions of users, and scale back down when traffic drops.

Recommended Resource

AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner Certification Course (Pass the Exam!) - freeCodeCamp

lessons.title: Identity & Access Management (IAM)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Security is job zero in the cloud. IAM is how you control who can access what inside your AWS account.

You should NEVER use the root account for daily tasks. Instead, create IAM Users, assign them to Groups, and use Policies (JSON documents) to grant the Principle of Least Privilege (giving users only the exact permissions they need to do their job).

lessons.title: Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2)
lessons.explanationHtml:
EC2 is the backbone of AWS. It provides raw, resizable compute capacity (Virtual Machines) in the cloud.

You choose the operating system (AMI), the instance type (e.g., heavily optimized for CPU vs RAM), and configure Security Groups to act as virtual firewalls controlling inbound and outbound traffic.
lessons.codeExample:
# Launching an EC2 instance via AWS CLI
aws ec2 run-instances \
    --image-id ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0 \
    --count 1 \
    --instance-type t2.micro \
    --key-name MyKeyPair \
    --security-group-ids sg-903004f8

lessons.title: Simple Storage Service (S3)
lessons.explanationHtml:
S3 provides infinite, highly durable object storage. You use it to store images, video files, backups, and even host static websites.

Unlike the hard drive on your computer (block storage), S3 stores files as "objects" in "buckets" and retrieves them via URLs. It is incredibly cheap and scales automatically.
lessons.codeExample:
# Upload a file to S3
aws s3 cp my-image.png s3://my-company-assets/images/

# Make it publicly readable (requires bucket policy)
aws s3api put-object-acl --bucket my-company-assets --key images/my-image.png --acl public-read

lessons.title: Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)
lessons.explanationHtml:
A VPC is your own logically isolated section of the AWS cloud. It is your private network.

You define the IP address range, create Subnets (public subnets for web servers, private subnets for databases), and configure Route Tables and Internet Gateways to control exactly how traffic flows in and out of your architecture.

lessons.title: Relational Database Service (RDS)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Managing database servers manually is a nightmare (backups, patching, scaling). RDS is a managed service that does this for you.

You can launch a fully configured MySQL, PostgreSQL, or SQL Server database in minutes, with automated daily backups and the ability to add "Read Replicas" to handle heavy traffic.

lessons.title: AWS Lambda (Serverless)
lessons.explanationHtml:
What if you didn't have to manage servers at all? AWS Lambda allows you to run code without provisioning or managing EC2 instances.

You upload your Node.js or Python code, and Lambda automatically scales out to run it whenever a specific event occurs (like an HTTP request or a file being uploaded to S3). You only pay for the exact milliseconds your code executes.

title: Docker & Containers
description: Stop saying 'It works on my machine'. Learn how to package your applications into portable containers that run perfectly anywhere.

lessons.title: What is a Container?
lessons.explanationHtml:
Before containers, we used Virtual Machines (VMs), which required running a full, heavy Operating System for every app. Containers share the host's OS kernel, making them incredibly lightweight and fast to start.

Docker packages your code, its dependencies, and its runtime environment into a single unit (an image) that is guaranteed to run exactly the same way on a developer's laptop as it does on a production server.

Recommended Resource

Docker Tutorial for Beginners - TechWorld with Nana

lessons.title: Writing a Dockerfile
lessons.explanationHtml:
A Dockerfile is a blueprint. It contains a list of instructions on how to build your container image.

You start with a base image (like a barebones Linux environment with Node.js installed), copy your code into the image, install your dependencies, and specify the command to run when the container starts.
lessons.codeExample:
FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json and install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install --production

# Copy the rest of the app
COPY . .

# Expose port and run
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

lessons.title: Building and Running Images
lessons.explanationHtml:
Once you have a Dockerfile, you use the docker build command to compile it into an Image. An Image is an immutable snapshot.

You then use docker run to spin up a running instance of that Image, which is called a Container. You must explicitly map ports from the container to your host machine if you want to access it.
lessons.codeExample:
# Build the image and tag it as 'my-app'
docker build -t my-app .

# Run the container in detached mode (-d)
# Map port 8080 on the host to 3000 in the container
docker run -d -p 8080:3000 my-app

lessons.title: Volumes (Persistent Data)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Containers are ephemeral. If you delete a database container, all the data inside it is destroyed forever!

To solve this, we use Docker Volumes. A Volume maps a folder inside the container to a permanent folder on your host machine's hard drive, ensuring data survives even if the container is destroyed.
lessons.codeExample:
# Run Postgres and mount a volume for data persistence
docker run -d \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=mysecretpassword \
  -v my-db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  postgres

lessons.title: Docker Compose
lessons.explanationHtml:
Modern apps rarely run in a single container. A web app needs a frontend, a backend API, and a database.

docker-compose.yml is a YAML file that allows you to define and run multi-container applications with a single command. It automatically creates a private network so the containers can talk to each other using their service names as URLs.
lessons.codeExample:
version: '3.8'
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
    depends_on: ["db"]
  db:
    image: postgres:15
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  pgdata:

title: Git & GitHub
description: Master version control. Learn how to track changes, collaborate with other developers, and manage code history safely.

lessons.title: Version Control Systems
lessons.explanationHtml:
Git is a version control system. It allows you to take "snapshots" (commits) of your code over time. If you break your project, you can instantly revert back to a previous, working snapshot.

GitHub is a website that hosts your Git repositories in the cloud, allowing multiple developers to collaborate on the same codebase simultaneously.

Recommended Resource

Git and GitHub for Beginners - freeCodeCamp

lessons.title: The Staging Area
lessons.explanationHtml:
When you edit files, Git notices the changes, but it doesn't automatically save them. You must explicitly "stage" the files you want to include in your next commit using git add.

This allows you to make 10 different changes, but logically group them into two separate, well-organized commits.
lessons.codeExample:
# See what files have changed
git status

# Stage specific files
git add index.html style.css

# Save the staged files into history with a message
git commit -m "Add header styling"

lessons.title: Branching Strategy
lessons.explanationHtml:
Never commit directly to the main branch. The main branch should always contain perfectly working, production-ready code.

When you want to build a new feature or fix a bug, you create a new Branch. This gives you an isolated sandbox to experiment. Once the feature is complete and tested, you merge it back into main.
lessons.codeExample:
# Create and switch to a new branch
git checkout -b feature/login-page

# Do work, add, and commit...

# Switch back to main
git checkout main

# Merge your feature into main
git merge feature/login-page

lessons.title: Pull Requests & Code Review
lessons.explanationHtml:
In a professional environment, you don't merge your own code. You push your branch to GitHub and open a Pull Request (PR).

A PR is a request for other developers to review your code. They can leave comments, request changes, and verify that your code meets company standards before approving the merge.
lessons.codeExample:
# Push your local branch to the remote GitHub repository
git push origin feature/login-page

# (Then go to github.com to open the PR)

lessons.title: Resolving Merge Conflicts
lessons.explanationHtml:
If you and a coworker edit the exact same line of the exact same file on different branches, Git won't know whose code to keep when you try to merge. This is a Merge Conflict.

Git will pause the merge and modify the file to show you both versions. You must manually delete the code you don't want, save the file, and commit the resolution.
